title: Invariant boundary control and arbitrary base change for marked nodal curves
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $B$ an integral finite-type $k$-scheme with generic point $\eta$, and $v:V\to B$ an H-projective flat finitely presented morphism. Suppose its geometric fibres are nonempty connected reduced nodal curves of pure dimension one, and its generic fibre is smooth geometrically integral. Suppose its fibres are quasi-split. Let $s_1,\ldots,s_n:B\to V$ be disjoint sections in the relative smooth locus, allowing $n=0$, and let a finite group $G$ act compatibly on $k,V,B,v$, preserving their union. Let $Z\subset V$ be a $G$-stable closed subset such that $Z\cap V_\eta\subseteq\bigcup_i s_i(\eta)$.

There is a $G$-stable nowhere dense closed subset $D\subset B$ such that $v$ is smooth over $B\setminus D$ and $Z\subseteq v^{-1}D\cup\bigcup_i s_i(B)$. More precisely one may take the union of the images of all irreducible components of $Z$ not dominating $B$, the image of the nonsmooth locus of $v$, and all $G$-translates of these images. Every component of $Z$ dominating $B$ is contained in the union of sections. If $B$ has dimension zero, this choice has $D=\varnothing$.

For every morphism $B'\to B$, the pulled-back family remains H-projective, flat and finitely presented, with nonempty connected reduced nodal geometric fibres of pure dimension one and quasi-split fibres. The pulled-back markings are disjoint sections in the relative smooth locus. The section equations and the boundary containment pull back, and the family is smooth over the inverse image of $B\setminus D$. This persistence requires neither a dominant morphism $B'\to B$ nor that the inverse image of $D$ be nowhere dense. No claim about smoothness of the generic fibre of an arbitrary such $B'$ is made. A nodal geometric curve has at each singular point completed geometric local ring $\Omega[[u,w]]/(uw)$; nodality, completion and power series mean [def-trf-nodal-geometric-fibres], [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] and [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], and pure dimension means [def-weil-pure-dimension].

Field, integrality, properness, finite type, geometric integrality, dimension, H-projectivity, finite morphisms, surjectivity, function fields and field extensions use [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-proper-morphism], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], [def-kun-projective], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-weil-surjective-morphism], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-field-extension] and [def-pc-field-tower]. H-projective means a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the target. Normal means all local rings are integrally closed domains. An alteration is a proper surjective morphism of integral schemes, with finite function-field extension and finite over a dense open. Actions may be nonfaithful and semilinear on the ground field; equivariance through a group surjection always includes its action on that field. Purely inseparable means every element has a characteristic-power in the smaller field in positive characteristic, and equality in characteristic zero. Flatness, finite presentation, smoothness, geometric fibres, closed immersions and fibre products use [def-weil-flat-morphism], [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], [def-weil-geometric-fibre], [def-weil-closed-immersion] and [def-pc-fibre-product]. Stable pointed curve means [def-sfb-stable-pointed-curve]; its sections may be permuted. Quasi-split means [def-sfb-quasi-split-nodal-fibres].

proof.text: Finite presentation includes quasi-compactness. Together with the given H-projective embedding this makes $v$ projective in the precise convention of [def-pc-projective-morphism]. Apply projective-implies-proper: $v$ is proper, hence separated, of finite type and a closed map (take the identity base change in universal closedness). A field is Noetherian since its only ideals are zero and the whole field, so $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is Noetherian. Apply finite-type-over-Noetherian first to $B\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and then to $v$ to obtain that $B,V$ are Noetherian. Thus the closed subset $Z$ is the union of finitely many irreducible components $C_1,\ldots,C_r$ of $Z$, each closed in $V$. Each section $s_i$ is a closed immersion since $v$ is separated. In particular $M=\bigcup_i s_i(B)$ is closed; when $n=0$ it is empty.

Let $C_j$ dominate $B$. By sobriety it has a generic point $c_j$, with $C_j=\overline{\{c_j\}}$. Continuity gives $v(C_j)\subseteq\overline{\{v(c_j)\}}$; dominance therefore says $\overline{\{v(c_j)\}}=B$. Uniqueness of the generic point of the integral scheme $B$ gives $v(c_j)=\eta$. The generic-boundary hypothesis now puts $c_j$ in $M$: the fibre of $M$ over $\eta$ is exactly the union of the marked points. Since $M$ is closed, $C_j=\overline{\{c_j\}}\subseteq M$. For each remaining component, $v(C_j)$ is closed by properness, is not all of $B$ by non-dominance, and hence does not contain $\eta$.

source.place: Tag 01IS (lemma-scheme-sober); de Jong Remark 2.5, p.603, horizontal versus vertical boundary components, expanded.

proof.text: Specialize the flat locally finitely presented smooth-locus lemma to the scheme morphism $v$. It gives the largest open $U\subseteq V$ on which $v$ is smooth; specializing its arbitrary-base-change clause to $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\eta)\to B$ gives that $U_\eta$ is the entire smooth locus of $V_\eta\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\eta)$. The generic fibre is smooth by hypothesis, so $U_\eta=V_\eta$. Consequently $N=V\setminus U$ is closed and has no point over $\eta$. Since $v$ is closed, $v(N)$ is closed and avoids $\eta$. This uses relative smoothness and the flat finite-presentation hypothesis; it uses no assumption that $k$ is perfect.

source.place: Tag 02V4 (lemma-set-points-where-fibres-smooth), case (1), with fibrewise description from 01V9 (lemma-smooth-at-point); the existing algebraic-space lemma specializes to schemes.

proof.text: Put $D_0=v(N)\cup\bigcup_{C_j\text{ not dominating }B}v(C_j)$ and $D=\bigcup_{g\in G}g(D_0)$. All unions are finite. Each $g$ acts by a homeomorphism of $B$, so all their terms are closed; each fixes its unique generic point, so every term avoids $\eta$. Thus $D$ is closed, $G$-stable, and nowhere dense: if a closed subset avoiding $\eta$ contained a nonempty open, that open would contain $\eta$, since $B$ is irreducible. The identity translate shows $D_0\subseteq D$. A component of $Z$ is either contained in $M$ by Step 2 or lies over $D_0$, giving $Z\subseteq M\cup v^{-1}D$. Moreover $v^{-1}(B\setminus D)\subseteq U$. The restriction of $v$ over $B\setminus D$ is the base change of the smooth morphism $U\to B$, so it is smooth. The construction is unchanged for semilinear actions: only the induced scheme automorphisms and the finite group law were used.

source.place: Tag 01VB (lemma-base-change-smooth); de Jong Remark 2.5, p.603, and Theorem 5.9 proof, p.617 (enlarge the base boundary by the nonsmooth image).

proof.text: If $\dim B=0$, its underlying space consists only of $\eta$. Indeed, a point $b\ne\eta$ would give a strict chain of nonempty irreducible closed subsets $\overline{\{b\}}\subsetneq B$ of length one: its closure cannot equal $B$ by uniqueness of the generic point. This contradicts dimension zero. A closed subset avoiding $\eta$ is therefore empty. In particular the very choice $D$ of Step 4 is empty, including when there are no markings or no components of $Z$.

source.place: Tag 0055 (definition-Krull); de Jong §3.3, field-base case, and Remark 2.5.

proof.text: Let $b:B'\to B$ be arbitrary, $V'=V\times_B B'$, with projections $q:V'\to V$ and $v':V'\to B'$. At every $x'\in V'$, flatness of $v$ at $q(x')$ implies flatness of $v'$ at $x'$ by pointwise base-change ascent; hence $v'$ is flat. Clause (3) of finite-presentation permanence gives finite presentation of $v'$, and projective base change applies to the projective morphism established in Step 1. Its conclusion is projective in [def-pc-projective-morphism], hence in particular H-projective. For a geometric point $t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to B'$, the fibre-product universal property identifies $(V')_t$ with $V_{bt}$ over the SAME algebraically closed field $\Omega$. Thus nonemptiness, connectedness, reducedness, nodality and pure dimension one are precisely the original geometric-fibre hypotheses, with no passage between geometric and ordinary fibre dimensions. The universal property gives $s'_i$ with $q s'_i=s_i b$ and $v's'_i=\mathrm{id}_{B'}$. If two section images met, projecting by $q$ would give a point in two original section images; thus they remain disjoint. The smooth-locus lemma gives $U_{v'}=q^{-1}U_v$. Since $q s'_i=s_i b$ and every $s_i$ lands in $U_v$, every $s'_i$ lands in $U_{v'}$. The same argument covers $n=0$ and empty $B'$.

source.place: Tags 01TS (lemma-base-change-finite-presentation), 01WF (lemma-H-projective-base-change), 02V4 (lemma-set-points-where-fibres-smooth); more-morphisms.tex 047C (lemma-flat-locus-base-change); cartesian geometric fibres and sections from the fibre-product universal property.

proof.text: Use only the standalone general base-change clause of the finite quasi-splitting lemma: for ANY quasi-split nodal family, quasi-splitting persists under arbitrary base change of its base. Applied to $v$ and $b$ it says that every singular point of each fibre of $v'$ and both normalization branches are rational over the new base residue field. This application needs neither normality nor projectivity of $B$, which occur only in the lemma's separate existence assertion about constructing a finite quasi-splitting cover. No such cover is constructed here.

source.place: Definition preceding Lemma 5.7, pp.614--615; base-change preservation in Theorem 5.9 proof, p.617; explicit general clause of the existing node.

proof.text: The universal property gives $s'_i:B'\to V'$ with $q s'_i=s_i b$ and $v's'_i=\mathrm{id}_{B'}$: the section equations pull back. The section square is cartesian by the same universal property. For its underlying images, let $x'\in q^{-1}(s_i(B))$. The map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x')\to V$ through $q$ factors through $s_i$: on an affine chart every element of the section's defining ideal vanishes in $\kappa(x')$, by the quotient-ring description of a closed immersion. Pair this factorization with $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x')\to B'$. Uniqueness for the fibre product gives $x'=s'_i(v'(x'))$. Conversely, $qs'_i=s_i b$ puts every $s'_i(B')$ in that inverse image. Thus $q^{-1}(M)=\bigcup_i s'_i(B')$. Pull back the set inclusion of Step 4 and use $vq=bv'$ to get $q^{-1}Z\subseteq(v')^{-1}(b^{-1}D)\cup\bigcup_i s'_i(B')$. The smooth family over $B\setminus D$ base changes to the restriction of $v'$ over $b^{-1}(B\setminus D)$, which is therefore smooth. None of these statements claims that $b^{-1}D$ is nowhere dense, that $B'$ is integral, or that a generic fibre of $v'$ is smooth. They apply also when $b$ lands inside $D$ (the asserted smooth open can then be empty) and when $B'$ is empty.
